title: The State of Home Cooking in 2026: 50+ Statistics & Trends That Define How America Eats
excerpt: A comprehensive look at the latest research on home cooking habits, generational differences, costs, and what's driving millions of Americans back to their kitchens.

content.text: Something remarkable is happening in American kitchens. Despite the convenience of food delivery apps, the proliferation of meal kits, and the persistent pull of restaurant dining, home cooking isn't just surviving - it's thriving in ways we haven't seen in decades. But what does the data actually tell us about how, why, and how often Americans are cooking at home in 2026?

I've spent weeks diving into the latest research, surveys, and statistics to paint a comprehensive picture of home cooking in America. What I found surprised me - and it will probably surprise you too. From generational cooking wars to the true cost savings of home cooking, here's what the numbers reveal about our relationship with the kitchen.
The Big Picture: How Many Americans Actually Cook?

Let's start with the headline numbers. According to the National Frozen & Refrigerated Foods Association's 2023 Eat at Home Report, 81% of consumers now cook more than half of their meals at home. That's a significant majority, suggesting that despite all the dining-out options available, the home kitchen remains the center of American eating habits.

content.label: Of Americans cook more than half their meals at home

content.text: Even more telling is what people expect to do going forward. HelloFresh's State of Home Cooking 2025-2026 report, conducted with Wakefield Research surveying 5,000 U.S. adults, found that 93% of Americans expect to cook as much or more in the coming year. Only 7% anticipate cooking less. The home cooking habit, it seems, is here to stay.

But the picture isn't entirely rosy. American Time Use Survey data shows that home-cooked meals dropped from 10.9 to 10 per week between 2018 and 2022. And compared to the pandemic peak, we're eating fewer home-cooked meals - though still more than before COVID-19 changed our relationship with restaurants.
The Generational Cooking Divide
Perhaps the most fascinating findings involve how different generations approach cooking. The data reveals a complex picture that challenges some assumptions while confirming others.

Gen Z cooks an average of 5.9 days per week, while Millennials lead at 6.7 days per week. Only 11% of Gen Z cooks every day, compared to 26% of Baby Boomers. Yet here's the twist: Gen Z actually enjoys cooking more than any other generation. Over half of Gen Z (51%) say they 'like' or 'love' meal preparation, compared to 46% overall.

content.title: Average Days Per Week Cooking by Generation
content.subtitle: Millennials lead in cooking frequency, while Gen Z cooks fewer days per week

content.label: Of Gen Z say they 'like' or 'love' cooking - more than any other generation

content.text: The confidence gap is real, though. Only 33% of Gen Z consider themselves skilled cooks, compared to 47% of Millennials. Nearly half (49%) of Gen Z are hesitant to cook for others because they lack cooking skills. This suggests a generation that wants to cook but feels they haven't yet developed the expertise.

Weekend cooking tells an interesting story about generational habits. 70% of Baby Boomers cook dinner from scratch every Sunday, compared to just 40% of Gen Z. Millennials lead in family meals, with 76% having sit-down dinners with others most or every day - higher than Gen Z (68%), Gen X (69%), or Boomers (67%).
Why People Are Cooking More: Money Talks

The number one driver of home cooking in 2026? Economics. According to a Flashfood survey conducted in December 2024, 83% of U.S. consumers report that saving money is a bigger priority in 2025 than it has been in other years. And 81% say saving money on food specifically is a priority for them this year.

content.label: Of Americans eating at home more to save money amid rising food costs

content.text: The financial impact is significant. When asked their top reason for cooking at home, 35% cite saving money, compared to 26% who cite nutrition. And 89% of consumers believe cooking meals at home is not only one of the best ways to save money on food but also a healthier alternative to takeout or dining out.

The inflation squeeze is real: 68% of Americans didn't buy a food item they usually get in the past 12 months because the price was too high. And 67% say rising prices over the last 12 months have made it harder to buy healthy food. Home cooking becomes not just a preference but a financial necessity.
The True Cost: Home Cooking vs. Eating Out

So what are the actual numbers? The data is striking. On average, a home-cooked meal costs around $4 to $6 per person, while a restaurant meal typically runs $15 to $20 or more. Americans save approximately $12 per meal by choosing to cook at home.

content.label: Average savings per meal when cooking at home vs. eating out

content.text: Annualized, that difference is staggering: it costs over $13,000 more per year to eat out compared to cooking the same meals at home. For families, the math becomes even more compelling.

The cost multipliers paint an even clearer picture. Restaurant delivery is 5 times more expensive than cooking at home. Meal kits, while convenient, are 3 times more expensive than cooking from scratch. Most restaurant meals cost 2 to 3 times their homemade equivalents - sometimes even more when delivery fees are involved.

content.title: Cost Comparison: How Much More Expensive?
content.subtitle: Percentage markup compared to cooking from scratch at home

content.text: Location matters too. New York residents see the most dramatic savings - $19.40 per meal by cooking at home. Residents in expensive states like New York, Connecticut, and Washington save at least $15 per meal compared to dining out.
Price Inflation: The Numbers Tell the Story

The inflation gap between home cooking and eating out has widened significantly. According to USDA data, the cost of food at home rose just 1.2% in 2024, while food away from home increased by 4.1% - more than three times the rate.

content.label: Restaurant food inflation vs. grocery inflation (Nov 2023-Nov 2024)

content.text: The Consumer Price Index tells a similar story: from November 2023 to November 2024, the cost of eating food away from home rose 3.6%, while food at home prices increased by only 1.6%. The economic case for home cooking continues to strengthen.
What's Stopping People from Cooking More?

Despite the financial incentives, barriers remain. The biggest culprits? Time and energy. According to HelloFresh's research, 1 in 5 adults skip cooking after work because they're simply too exhausted. Lack of time (20%) and after-work fatigue (19%) are the biggest reasons people say they don't cook more.

There's also the phenomenon of 'meal repeating.' A striking 86% of Americans are 'meal repeaters,' eating the same meals over and over at least some of the time. While 60% do so because it ensures everyone gets what they like, 21% admit it's because they lack the energy to cook a new recipe.

content.label: Of Americans are 'meal repeaters' who eat the same dishes regularly

content.text: The day of the week matters too. 61% of Americans cook at home on Mondays, but that drops to 49% by Friday. The weekend cooking gap suggests that by the end of the work week, restaurant and takeout options become more appealing.
The Social Media Influence on Cooking

TikTok has become a dominant force in shaping how Americans cook. Food-related hashtags on the platform have amassed over 4.5 million posts. The 'Girl Dinner' trend alone garnered more than 281,000 posts celebrating casual, deconstructed meals.

The platform's influence extends beyond inspiration to actual purchasing behavior. One TikTok trend contributed to a 15.9% increase in cottage cheese sales in the United States. By May 2024, UK stores reported 22-30% increases compared to the previous year. The 'Sleepy Girl Mocktail' trend drove notable increases in tart cherry juice sales during Dry January 2024.

content.label: Increase in cottage cheese sales driven by TikTok trends

content.text: What makes food trends go viral? Researchers point to eye-catching visuals, ease of replication, emotional engagement, and TikTok's algorithm favoring visually appealing, shareable content. For home cooks, this means accessible recipes that look good on camera are more likely to end up in real kitchens.
The Meal Kit Revolution

The meal kit industry continues its remarkable growth. In 2024, the global market reached $21.99 billion, up from $18.83 billion in 2023. Projections suggest it will hit $25-30 billion in 2025 and could reach $80-114 billion by 2033.
In the U.S. specifically, the industry hit $9.1 billion in 2025, with HelloFresh dominating at 74-78% market share. Home Chef holds about 12% of the market, with Blue Apron at 6%.

content.title: U.S. Meal Kit Market Share
content.subtitle: HelloFresh dominates the American meal kit industry

content.label: U.S. meal kit market size in 2025

content.text: Americans are embracing shortcuts. 81% use conveniences like meal prep kits or ready-to-eat meals to get a hot meal on the table more easily. 39% use these shortcuts at least once weekly, with Millennials leading at 50% weekly usage. The industry is responding with more subscription flexibility - an estimated 72.6% of the market in 2025.
The Post-Pandemic Kitchen

The pandemic fundamentally changed how Americans relate to their kitchens. During COVID-19, 60% of Americans cooked at home more than before. 44% reported cooking more often since the pandemic started, and 25% cooked more with family members.

But have those habits stuck? The data is mixed. Americans are returning to pre-pandemic patterns, with North Americans eating 8.4 home-cooked meals per week in 2022 - the same rate as 2019. The U.S. specifically hit a 'historic low' of 8.2 meals per week, compared to 9.4 during the pandemic peak in 2020.

content.title: Home-Cooked Meals Per Week in the U.S.
content.subtitle: The pandemic spike has normalized, but remains above pre-2018 levels

content.label: Home-cooked meals per week in the U.S. - a historic low

content.text: Still, 64% of Americans continue cooking at home to save money and control their budget. The pandemic may not have permanently transformed us into a nation of home cooks, but it did create a baseline appreciation for the kitchen that persists.
What America Is Actually Cooking

When Americans do cook, what are they making? Mexican cuisine ranks as the most popular homemade cuisine in the United States, followed by American classics. As of mid-2024, hamburgers, french fries, and grilled cheese sandwiches were the most popular American dishes, with about 84% of respondents having positive opinions of each.

Mediterranean cuisine continues to gain ground, dominating both home and restaurant cooking trends. Asian-inspired dishes and flavors are also rising, particularly among younger cooks influenced by social media trends.

Home cooks are getting more adventurous with heat. They're moving beyond the humble jalapeño to explore pepper-based condiments from around the world - sambal, piri piri, gochujang, and hatch green chiles are all trending in home kitchens.
Looking Ahead: The Future of Home Cooking

What does the future hold? Five years after the pandemic redefined our relationship with the kitchen, several trends are clear. Economic pressure will continue driving home cooking adoption. Social media will keep influencing what and how we cook. And the generational gap in cooking skills will likely narrow as Gen Z gains experience.

The 93% of Americans who expect to maintain or increase their home cooking represent a fundamental shift in how we think about meals. Home cooking isn't just a fallback when budgets get tight - it's becoming a lifestyle choice, a creative outlet, and a way to take control of both health and finances.

In the wake of the pandemic, many people rediscovered home cooking as a mindful ritual that fosters connection, creativity, and well-being. Five years later, mealtime continues to evolve as Americans adapt to shifting lifestyles, wellness trends, new technologies, and economic pressures.
content.author: HelloFresh State of Home Cooking 2025-2026 Report

content.text: The numbers tell a clear story: despite every convenience modern life offers, the home kitchen remains central to American life. Whether driven by economics, health, creativity, or simply the pleasure of a home-cooked meal, Americans are cooking - and they don't plan to stop.
Sources and Methodology

This article synthesizes data from multiple sources including: HelloFresh State of Home Cooking 2025-2026 Report (Wakefield Research, 5,000 U.S. adults), Flashfood Survey (December 2024, 2,089 adults), Instacart Cooking Survey (September 2025, 1,011 U.S. adults), NFRA Eat at Home Report, Bureau of Labor Statistics American Time Use Survey, USDA Food Price Data, Consumer Price Index, FMI research on Gen Z cooking habits, and various industry market reports from Grand View Research, Straits Research, and IBISWorld.

title: The Incredible Journey of the Tomato: From Poison to Passion
excerpt: How a feared 'poison apple' became one of the world's most beloved ingredients, transforming cuisines from Italy to India.

content.text: Let me tell you something that still amazes me after thirty years in the kitchen. That beautiful, ruby-red tomato sitting on your cutting board? The one you're about to slice for your salad or simmer into a rich Sunday sauce? People were once terrified of it. Absolutely terrified. They called it the 'poison apple' and wouldn't dare let it touch their lips.

It is worth sitting with how strange that is. The tomato is so central to Italian cooking that the two are hard to separate in the imagination, and yet for the better part of two centuries after it arrived from the Americas, Italians grew the plant and would not eat the fruit. Botanists filed it alongside deadly nightshade, which it genuinely does resemble, and the suspicion stuck for generations.
Born in the Mountains of Peru

The tomato's story begins high in the Andes Mountains of South America, in what is now Peru and Ecuador. Wild tomatoes still grow there today, tiny little things no bigger than your thumbnail, nothing like the beefsteaks and heirlooms we know. The indigenous peoples of these regions had been cultivating and eating tomatoes for thousands of years before any European ever laid eyes on one.

The Aztecs were the real tomato enthusiasts of the ancient world. They grew them in their famous floating gardens called chinampas, and they had a word for them: 'tomatl,' meaning 'the swelling fruit.' They combined tomatoes with chili peppers, ground them together with a stone mortar, and created what we'd recognize today as the ancestor of salsa. Imagine that - salsa has been around for over a thousand years.

content.label: Tomatoes have been cultivated in the Americas

content.text: When I make a fresh pico de gallo in my kitchen, I like to think I'm continuing a tradition that stretches back to those Aztec cooks. The technique hasn't changed much - good tomatoes, fresh chilies, a bit of salt. Sometimes the old ways really are the best ways.
The Europeans Get Nervous

Here's where the story gets interesting. When Spanish conquistadors arrived in Mexico in the early 1500s, they encountered tomatoes and thought, 'Well, these look interesting.' They brought seeds back to Spain, and from there, tomatoes spread across Europe. But nobody wanted to eat them.

You see, Europeans noticed something troubling. Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family, the same family that includes deadly belladonna and poisonous mandrake. The leaves of the tomato plant do contain toxins. So people looked at this strange new fruit and thought, 'No thank you, I'd rather not die today.'
For roughly two centuries, Europeans grew tomatoes and refused to eat them. The fruit was admired in gardens and suspected at the table.

There's another part of this story that's grimly fascinating. Wealthy Europeans ate from pewter plates, which contained high levels of lead. When acidic tomatoes touched these plates, they'd leach lead into the food. People would eat tomatoes, get sick from lead poisoning, and blame the tomato. The poor, who ate from wooden plates, didn't have this problem - but nobody thought to make that connection.
Italy Falls in Love

Thank goodness for the Italians. If it weren't for them, we might still be treating tomatoes as ornamental plants. The warm Mediterranean climate was perfect for growing tomatoes, and Italian peasants - eating from clay and wooden dishes - discovered they could enjoy this fruit without dropping dead.

The first Italian cookbook to include tomato recipes appeared in 1692. A chef named Antonio Latini wrote about cooking tomatoes 'in the Spanish style,' which tells you something about how new and exotic they still seemed. But the Italians took to tomatoes like nothing else. Within a hundred years, they had become essential to Italian cooking.

content.label: First recorded recipe for pasta with tomato sauce

content.text: Now here's a fact that surprises everyone: pasta with tomato sauce - that dish we think of as the most Italian thing in the world - didn't really exist until the 1800s. Pasta had been around for centuries, tomatoes had been around for centuries, but putting them together? That was a relatively recent invention. The first known recipe for pasta al pomodoro appeared in 1839 in Naples.

I cook a simple tomato sauce almost every week. Just tomatoes, garlic, olive oil, basil, and a pinch of salt. Nothing fancy. And every time I do, I think about how this simple combination took humanity thousands of years to figure out. We came so close to never discovering it at all.
The Tomato Goes Global

Once people finally accepted that tomatoes wouldn't kill them, there was no stopping this fruit. It spread across the globe with remarkable speed. Today, tomatoes are grown in virtually every country on Earth, and they're the second most consumed vegetable worldwide, right after potatoes.

Think about how many cuisines depend on tomatoes now. Italian, obviously. Mexican, of course - they had them first. But also Indian curries, Greek salads, Middle Eastern stews, American everything. Ketchup alone is a multi-billion dollar industry. The tomato went from being feared to being absolutely indispensable.

content.label: Tomatoes grown worldwide in 2023, according to the FAO

content.text: When I shop for tomatoes at the farmers market in late summer, I always look for the ugliest ones. The ones with cracks and odd shapes and that deep, almost purple-red color. Those are the ones with the most flavor. Those are the ones that would make those old Aztec farmers proud.

The next time you bite into a ripe tomato, still warm from the sun, I want you to think about its journey. From the high mountains of Peru, across the ocean to a fearful Europe, through centuries of suspicion, and finally to your plate. That's quite a trip for a little red fruit. And aren't we lucky that someone, somewhere, was brave enough to take that first bite?

title: The Potato That Changed the World: A Story of Survival and Civilization
excerpt: From Incan treasure to Irish tragedy, discover how the humble potato shaped empires, sparked revolutions, and fed billions.

content.text: I've cooked thousands of potatoes in my career. Mashed them, roasted them, fried them, baked them. I've turned them into silky French purees and crispy breakfast hash. But it wasn't until I traveled to Peru that I truly understood what a potato could be - and what it has meant to human history.

High in the Andes, at altitudes where most crops simply refuse to grow, farmers still cultivate potatoes in varieties most of the world has never seen. Purple ones, yellow ones, red ones, some shaped like fingers, others twisted and knobbled. Peru’s International Potato Center holds thousands of native varieties, the product of roughly eight thousand years of selection by Andean farmers. That is longer than the pyramids have been standing.
The Sacred Tuber of the Incas

The potato was first cultivated in Peru around 8,000 BC, making it one of humanity's oldest food crops. The Incas didn't just eat potatoes - they worshipped them. They buried potatoes with their dead. They created pottery shaped like potatoes. They even measured time based on how long it took to cook different potato varieties.

content.label: Potato varieties developed by Andean farmers

content.text: What amazed me most was learning about chuño, an ancient Incan technique for preserving potatoes. Farmers would leave potatoes out at night to freeze, then stomp on them during the day to squeeze out moisture, repeating this process for several days until they had dried potato chunks that could last for years. This was freeze-drying, invented thousands of years before we had freezers. The Incas fed their armies with chuño during long military campaigns. You could say the potato helped build an empire.

In my restaurant, I serve a dish inspired by those Andean potatoes - roasted purple potatoes with herbs from my garden. It's simple, but every time I plate it, I think about those farmers in Peru, still growing potatoes the way their ancestors did, thousands of years ago.
Europe Says No Thanks

When Spanish conquistadors brought potatoes back to Europe in the 1570s, Europeans looked at this strange underground vegetable and wanted nothing to do with it. Sound familiar? Just like the tomato, the potato was met with deep suspicion.

People didn't trust food that grew underground - it seemed dark and mysterious. The potato wasn't mentioned anywhere in the Bible, which made some religious folks nervous. And because it was a member of the nightshade family, with those slightly toxic leaves, people worried it might be poisonous. For nearly two hundred years, potatoes in Europe were mostly fed to livestock.
It took royal decrees, staged thefts and a good deal of hunger to talk Europe into eating the potato. Fear went first, then the famine came anyway.

The change came slowly. Frederick the Great of Prussia ordered peasants to plant potatoes, threatening to cut off the noses and ears of those who refused. In France, a clever pharmacist named Antoine-Augustin Parmentier convinced King Louis XVI to post armed guards around potato fields, making people think they must be valuable. When curious citizens snuck in at night to steal potatoes, the plan worked perfectly. The French finally started eating potatoes.
Ireland's Love and Tragedy

Nowhere did the potato become more important than in Ireland. The climate was perfect for growing them, and unlike grain, potatoes couldn't be easily taxed by English landlords. A small plot of land could produce enough potatoes to feed a family. By the 1800s, the Irish had become almost completely dependent on this single crop.

I've cooked with Irish chefs who talk about the potato with a kind of reverence mixed with sorrow. They know what happened next. In 1845, a water mold called Phytophthora infestans arrived in Ireland, spreading through potato fields like wildfire. It turned healthy potatoes into black, rotting mush within days.

content.label: People died during the Irish Potato Famine

content.text: The Great Famine lasted six years. Over a million people died from starvation and disease. Another million fled Ireland, many coming to America, forever changing the demographics of both countries. The population of Ireland dropped by 25 percent and has never fully recovered.

When I make colcannon - that traditional Irish dish of mashed potatoes with cabbage and butter - I think about this history. Food carries memory. Food carries grief. That simple bowl of mashed potatoes connects to a tragedy that shaped millions of lives.
The Potato Feeds the World

Despite that devastating chapter, the potato went on to become one of the most important foods on Earth. Today, it's the fourth largest food crop in the world, after rice, wheat, and maize. China grows more potatoes than any other country, followed by India and Russia. Over a billion people worldwide eat potatoes every day.

And the variety is staggering. From the thin-skinned fingerlings I use for roasting, to the starchy Russets that make perfect baked potatoes, to the waxy Yukon Golds that shine in a gratin. Each variety has its own personality, its own purpose in the kitchen.

content.label: Potatoes grown worldwide in 2023, according to the FAO

content.text: In my kitchen, I treat potatoes with the respect they deserve. I buy them from local farmers when I can. I store them in a cool, dark place. And I never, ever call them boring. There's nothing boring about a food that has fed armies, built empires, caused mass migrations, and continues to nourish billions of people every single day.

The humble potato. It looks so ordinary sitting there on your counter. But it carries eight thousand years of human history inside it. That's the thing about ingredients - they're never just ingredients. They're stories waiting to be told.

title: How Italian Cuisine Conquered the World: A 2,000-Year Journey
excerpt: From ancient Roman feasts to modern pizzerias, trace the remarkable evolution of Italy's most exported cultural treasure.

content.text: Ask anyone to name the most popular cuisine in the world, and most will say Italian. Pizza shops on every corner. Pasta in every supermarket. Tiramisu on every dessert menu. Italian food has become so universal that we barely think about how extraordinary that is. How did the cooking of one small Mediterranean country come to dominate dinner tables from Tokyo to Toronto?

I've spent a lot of time cooking Italian food and even more time thinking about it. What I've come to understand is that Italian cuisine isn't really one thing - it's dozens of regional cuisines that share some common threads. And the Italian food we eat today would have been completely unrecognizable to Italians just a few centuries ago.
What the Romans Ate

Let's start at the beginning - ancient Rome. The Romans were serious about food. They wrote cookbooks. They threw elaborate dinner parties that lasted for hours. They imported ingredients from across their vast empire. But their food was nothing like modern Italian cooking.

The Romans loved garum, a fermented fish sauce they put on everything. Think of it like ancient ketchup - a universal condiment. They sweetened their dishes with honey because refined sugar didn't exist yet. They ate a lot of grain porridge called puls, which was the staple food of the common people. No tomatoes, no peppers, no potatoes - all of those were still thousands of miles away in the Americas, waiting to be discovered.

What the Romans did establish was a culture that valued good eating. They believed that food should be pleasurable, that meals should be social occasions, that ingredients mattered. This attitude - this belief that cooking is worth taking seriously - would carry through the centuries and become central to Italian identity.
The Regional Divide

After the fall of the Roman Empire, Italy fragmented into dozens of city-states, each developing its own culinary identity. This is important to understand because there really was no such thing as 'Italian food' for most of history. There was Tuscan food, Sicilian food, Venetian food, Neapolitan food - each one distinct and proud.
There is no single Italian cuisine. There are regions that have been arguing about food for longer than Italy has been a country.

The north used butter; the south used olive oil. The coast ate seafood; the mountains ate meat and cheese. These differences still exist today. A Bolognese cook would never put garlic in their ragù, while a Neapolitan cook couldn't imagine sauce without it. Both would insist their way is the only correct way.

I love this about Italian cooking. Every dish has a home, a family, a story. When you eat cacio e pepe, you're eating Rome. When you eat pesto, you're eating Genoa. When you eat arancini, you're eating Sicily. The geography is built right into the recipes.
The New World Changes Everything

Then came 1492, and everything changed. Columbus sailed west looking for spices and found a whole hemisphere of new ingredients. Slowly, tomatoes, peppers, and corn began arriving in Italy. At first, nobody knew what to do with them. It took generations for Italians to figure out how these strange new foods fit into their cooking.

The tomato's story in Italy is particularly amazing to me. Italians were suspicious of tomatoes for almost two hundred years. They grew them as ornamental plants. They thought they might be poisonous. But eventually, someone in Naples took a chance, cooked them down into a sauce, and history was made.

content.label: First recipe for pasta with tomato sauce was published

content.text: Think about that date - 1839. Pasta with tomato sauce, the dish we think of as the most quintessentially Italian thing in the world, was invented more recently than the United States of America. It's not an ancient tradition; it's a relatively modern one. But Italians made it so perfectly their own that we can't imagine it any other way.
Pizza Takes Over the Planet

No food has spread more successfully than pizza. It started as street food for the poor in Naples - just flatbread with tomato and maybe some cheese. The most famous story is that pizza Margherita was created in 1889 for Queen Margherita of Italy, with toppings in the colors of the Italian flag: red tomatoes, white mozzarella, green basil. Whether that story is true or not, it makes for a great legend.

Italian immigrants brought pizza to America in the late 1800s, and it evolved in new directions. New York style, Chicago deep dish, California with its fancy toppings. Japan has pizza topped with mayonnaise and corn. Brazil puts peas on pizza. Some Italians are horrified by these variations; others just shrug and say that's what happens when good food travels.

content.label: Pizzas sold worldwide every year

content.text: In my own cooking, I try to stay close to traditional techniques while accepting that traditions themselves were once innovations. The Italians who first put tomato on pizza were breaking with tradition. The ones who added mozzarella were experimenting. Every dish we now consider classic was once someone's crazy new idea.
Why Italian Food Took Over

So why did Italian cuisine become so globally dominant? I have a few theories. First, Italian food is built on a philosophy that great cooking doesn't require complexity - it requires great ingredients handled simply. A perfect plate of spaghetti with garlic and oil has just five ingredients. That simplicity is accessible to home cooks everywhere.

Second, Italian immigrants spread across the globe, bringing their recipes with them. They opened restaurants. They shared their food with neighbors. They adapted to local ingredients while keeping core techniques intact. Italian food is resilient enough to travel well.

Third, and maybe most important, Italian food just tastes good. The combination of wheat, tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, and cheese hits something fundamental in human taste preferences. It's satisfying. It's comforting. It feels like home, even if you've never been to Italy.

When I make a batch of fresh pasta in my kitchen, rolling the dough through my hand-cranked machine, I feel connected to a long tradition. But I also know that tradition is more flexible than we sometimes think. Italian cuisine conquered the world by being itself while allowing itself to change. That's a lesson for any cook.

title: The Spice Trade That Shaped History: Wars, Wealth, and World Exploration
excerpt: How the quest for pepper, cinnamon, and cloves drove European exploration, built empires, and transformed global cuisine forever.

content.text: I keep a small bowl of whole spices on my counter - peppercorns, cinnamon sticks, cardamom pods, whole cloves. They cost me maybe ten dollars, and I barely think about it. But five hundred years ago, those same spices could have bought you a house. Countries went to war over them. Explorers sailed into uncharted waters searching for them. The entire map of the modern world was drawn, in large part, by the human desire to make food taste better.

This is the story of the spice trade, and it's one of the most dramatic tales in all of culinary history. When people ask me why I'm so fascinated by food history, this is the example I give. Food isn't just what we eat - it's what drove us to explore the globe.
The Mysterious Origins

For thousands of years, Europeans knew that spices existed but had almost no idea where they came from. Arab traders controlled the spice routes and kept their sources fiercely secret. They spread wild stories to discourage anyone from looking too hard - cinnamon grew in deep canyons guarded by winged serpents, they said. Cassia was found in shallow lakes protected by fearsome bats.

These stories seem silly to us now, but they worked. For centuries, Europeans paid astronomical prices for spices without ever knowing they came from a few small islands in what is now Indonesia. The Arab traders maintained their monopoly, and spices remained mysterious luxuries.

content.label: Estimated age of the international spice trade

content.text: In my kitchen, I think about this history whenever I open my spice cabinet. That jar of cinnamon comes from Sri Lanka, originally called Ceylon. That pepper comes from the Malabar Coast of India. That nutmeg comes from the Banda Islands of Indonesia - a place so small and remote that most people couldn't find it on a map, yet it was once one of the most valuable pieces of real estate on Earth.
Worth More Than Gold

Just how valuable were spices? Let me put it this way: peppercorns were counted individually, like jewels. Rent could be paid in pepper. Dowries included pepper. When Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 AD, the ransom demanded included 3,000 pounds of pepper. This was not a condiment; this was currency.

Nutmeg was even more precious. In the 1600s, a small bag of nutmeg could set you up for life. A single ship full of nutmeg could make everyone aboard wealthy. The Dutch, who controlled the nutmeg trade for a time, considered the Banda Islands more valuable than Manhattan - they actually traded one for the other.
Spices were never only flavour. They were medicine, preservative, status and currency, and empires were built and lost over control of them.

Why did Europeans want spices so badly? Partly for flavor, certainly. Medieval European food could be bland, and spices made it exciting. But spices also preserved food before refrigeration, masked the taste of meat that was past its prime, and signaled wealth and sophistication. If you could serve heavily spiced food, you were telling your guests that you could afford the finest things.
The Race to Find the Source

Everything changed when Europeans decided to find the spices themselves. The Portuguese led the way. In 1498, Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India, breaking the Arab monopoly on the spice trade. When he returned to Lisbon, his cargo of pepper and cinnamon sold for sixty times what the voyage had cost. The race was on.

Columbus sailed west in 1492 specifically looking for a new route to the spice islands. He found the Americas instead - a happy accident that would transform the world, but a disappointment at the time. He kept insisting, even when the evidence suggested otherwise, that he was near China and the spice lands.

content.label: Magellan's expedition circumnavigated the globe seeking spices

content.text: Magellan's expedition finally reached the Spice Islands by sailing west, proving it could be done. Of the five ships and 270 men who started that voyage, only one ship and 18 men returned. But that ship, the Victoria, was loaded with cloves - enough to pay for the entire expedition many times over. Spices were worth dying for, apparently.
The Dark Side of the Trade

I'd be lying if I told you this story was just about adventure and flavor. The spice trade brought tremendous suffering to the people who actually grew the spices. The Dutch East India Company, formed to control the spice trade, became history's most valuable corporation - worth over seven trillion dollars in today's money. They achieved this through brutal means.

On the Banda Islands, the Dutch massacred or enslaved nearly the entire population to control nutmeg production. They burned spice trees on other islands to keep supply low and prices high. The colonization of Indonesia, India, and much of Asia was driven largely by the desire to control spices. We're still dealing with the consequences of these actions today.
When I cook with spices now, I try to buy from fair trade sources. It seems like the least I can do, given this history. The pepper in my grinder shouldn't cost someone their freedom.
Spices Today

The spice trade eventually collapsed as spices were planted around the world, breaking monopolies. Prices fell. What once could buy a house now costs a few dollars at the supermarket. Pepper is so common we barely notice it.

But think about what remains: trade routes that became modern shipping lanes, colonial boundaries that became national borders, corporations that became models for global business. The world we live in was shaped by the desire for flavor. Every time I grind pepper over my dinner, I'm connected to that history.

content.label: Global spice trade value today

content.text: In my kitchen, I treat spices with respect. I buy them whole and grind them fresh. I store them away from heat and light. I use them generously but thoughtfully. These little seeds and barks and dried flowers once drove men to sail across oceans and risk everything. They deserve a little reverence.

title: Plant-Based Nutrition: What the Latest Research Actually Says
excerpt: A comprehensive look at recent scientific studies on plant-based diets, their health benefits, and what the data reveals about this growing food movement.

content.text: Twenty years ago, when I told other chefs I was interested in plant-based cooking, they looked at me like I'd lost my mind. 'Where's the protein?' they'd ask. 'What about B12? Don't you miss bacon?' These days, I hear those same questions from home cooks trying to make sense of all the headlines about plant-based diets.

Here's the thing: there's a lot of noise out there, a lot of passionate opinions on both sides. But there's also actual science - peer-reviewed studies, long-term data, careful research. Let me walk you through what we actually know about plant-based eating, based on evidence rather than ideology.
What the Research Shows

The scientific literature on plant-based diets has exploded in the past decade. We now have large, well-designed studies tracking hundreds of thousands of people over many years. And the results are pretty consistent: eating more plants is associated with better health outcomes.

The largest study of its kind followed 209,298 American health professionals for up to two decades. Those whose diets scored highest on a healthful plant based index, meaning more whole grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts and legumes, had substantially lower rates of coronary heart disease. The comparison was not strict vegans against meat eaters. It was the overall pattern of eating more plants, and eating better ones, which is a far more achievable target.

I want to be clear about something: eating 'more plants' doesn't mean eating 'zero meat.' Some of the healthiest traditional diets in the world, like the Mediterranean diet, include modest amounts of fish and even some red meat. The key seems to be making plants the star of the plate, not eliminating animal products entirely.
The Gut Connection

One of the most exciting areas of recent research involves the gut microbiome - the trillions of bacteria living in your digestive system. It turns out these little creatures have a huge influence on your health, and they love fiber. They thrive on the complex carbohydrates found in vegetables, whole grains, and legumes.

A Stanford trial put 36 healthy adults on either a high fibre or a high fermented food diet for ten weeks. The fermented food group saw their gut microbial diversity climb and nineteen inflammatory markers fall, including interleukin 6. The fibre group, to the researchers’ surprise, saw neither over that period. The honest reading is that fermented foods did something measurable in ten weeks and fibre needs longer, not that fibre does not matter.
The interesting question is not whether a plant based diet can work. It is which parts of it need planning, and B12 is the honest answer.

In my cooking, I try to incorporate as many different plant foods as possible. A stir-fry with five different vegetables. A salad with three kinds of leafy greens. A grain bowl with lentils, chickpeas, and seeds. Variety isn't just more interesting to eat; it appears to be better for your gut.
The Practical Questions
Okay, so more plants are good for you. But what about the practical concerns? These are the questions I hear most often, so let me address them directly.

Protein: Plants have plenty of protein. Lentils, beans, tofu, tempeh, seitan, nuts, seeds - all excellent sources. The idea that you need to carefully combine proteins at every meal has been debunked. Just eat a variety of plant foods throughout the day, and you'll get all the amino acids you need.

Vitamin B12: This is the one nutrient you really do need to watch on a purely plant-based diet. B12 comes from bacteria and is found reliably only in animal products. If you're eating vegan, you should take a B12 supplement or consume B12-fortified foods. This is non-negotiable.

Iron: Plant-based iron isn't absorbed as easily as iron from meat, but you can boost absorption by eating iron-rich foods with vitamin C. That's why beans with tomatoes, or spinach with lemon, are such classic combinations. Our ancestors figured this out long before they understood the science.
Beyond Personal Health

I'd be leaving out an important part of the story if I didn't mention the environmental research. The data here is also quite clear: plant-based diets have significantly smaller environmental footprints than meat-heavy diets.

A 2018 Oxford study found that shifting to a plant-based diet could reduce an individual's food-related carbon footprint by up to 73%. That's enormous. It's probably the single biggest thing most of us can do to reduce our environmental impact.

content.title: Dietary carbon footprint, relative to high meat eaters
content.subtitle: UK cohort of 55,000 people, Scarborough et al., Nature Food, 2023

content.text: Now, I'm a chef, not an environmental scientist. But I do think about where my food comes from and what impact it has. These days, when I design menus, I naturally lean toward plant-forward dishes. It's better for health, better for the planet, and - when done well - absolutely delicious.
Finding Your Own Balance

Here's my advice, for whatever it's worth: don't get too caught up in labels. You don't have to call yourself vegan or vegetarian or flexitarian. Just try to eat more plants. More vegetables, more fruits, more legumes, more whole grains. Make meat a supporting player rather than the star of every meal.

The research supports this moderate approach. You don't have to be perfect. You don't have to give up everything you love. Just shift the balance, bit by bit, toward more plants. Your body - and your gut bacteria - will thank you.

title: The Global Journey of Curry: From India to Every Kitchen
excerpt: How a blend of spices from the Indian subcontinent traveled the world, adapting and evolving to become one of humanity's favorite foods.

content.text: The word 'curry' is both precise and hopelessly vague. Ask a chef in Chennai what curry means and they'll describe something completely different from a chef in Tokyo, who'll describe something completely different from a chef in London. This one word covers thousands of dishes across dozens of countries. It's a culinary category so broad that it almost becomes meaningless - and yet we all know what it means when someone says they're craving curry.

I've cooked curries from many traditions - Indian butter chicken, Thai green curry, Japanese katsu curry, Jamaican goat curry, Malaysian rendang. Each one is unique. Each one claims its own history. But they're all connected by a common thread: the idea that spices, combined thoughtfully, can transform simple ingredients into something magical.
Where It All Began

The story starts in India, where people have been cooking with complex spice blends for at least four thousand years. Archaeological evidence from the ancient Indus Valley civilization shows that people were grinding turmeric, ginger, and garlic together thousands of years before anyone called it curry.

The word 'curry' itself probably comes from 'kari,' a Tamil word meaning sauce or gravy. When British colonizers arrived in India, they heard this word and applied it, rather loosely, to any Indian dish with sauce. This was a simplification, of course. Indian cooks didn't have a single category called 'curry' - they had hundreds of specific dishes, each with its own name and tradition.

content.label: History of spiced cooking in India

content.text: In traditional Indian cooking, there's no such thing as 'curry powder.' Each dish has its own specific blend of spices, mixed fresh for that particular recipe. A chicken korma uses different spices than a lamb vindaloo, which uses different spices than a vegetable curry. The British invention of a standardized 'curry powder' was convenient for colonial households but completely missed the point of Indian spice craft.
The Colonial Spread

As European powers colonized Asia, curry traditions traveled along colonial trade routes. The British brought their version of Indian curry back to England, where it was adapted to local tastes - less spicy, more gravy, served with rice that had been boiled until soft. This Anglo-Indian cuisine developed its own character, becoming something new.

One of my favorite curry origin stories involves chicken tikka masala. This dish, now served in Indian restaurants worldwide, was probably invented in Britain. The legend goes that a customer complained their chicken tikka was too dry, so the chef added tomato soup to create a sauce. Is the story true? Who knows. But it captures something real about how curries evolve when they travel.
Curry is less a recipe than a way of thinking about spice. That is exactly why it travelled so far and came back changed.

The Japanese curry story is equally fascinating. British naval officers brought curry to Japan in the late 1800s, and the Japanese adapted it into something entirely their own - sweeter, milder, thickened with roux, served over rice with pickled ginger on the side. Today, curry rice is one of Japan's most popular comfort foods, served everywhere from school cafeterias to high-end restaurants.
Thai Curry: A Different Path

Thai curries developed on a completely separate track from Indian curries. While they share the concept of complex spice pastes, Thai curries rely on fresh herbs, coconut milk, and different flavor profiles. Green curry gets its color from fresh green chilies and herbs. Red curry uses dried red chilies. Yellow curry includes turmeric but is otherwise quite different from Indian preparations.

I love making Thai curry pastes from scratch. Pounding chilies, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste in a mortar and pestle creates a fragrance that fills the entire kitchen. It's labor-intensive, but there's no substitute for that fresh, bright flavor. Store-bought paste is fine in a pinch, but it's never quite the same.

The Thai curry tradition shows that 'curry' is really about technique and approach rather than specific ingredients. It's about layering flavors, building complexity, balancing heat with other tastes. These principles can be applied to ingredients from anywhere.
Curry Today

Today, curry has become truly global. You'll find curry in Trinidad, where Indian indentured servants brought their cooking traditions after slavery was abolished. You'll find it in South Africa, where Durban's bunny chow - curry served in a hollowed-out bread loaf - has become iconic. You'll find it in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, each country putting its own spin on spiced, saucy dishes.

In my own cooking, I've stopped worrying about authenticity and started focusing on deliciousness. I'll use Indian spices with Thai techniques. I'll add Japanese curry roux to an Indian-spiced stew. Curry is a living tradition, always changing, always adapting. That's what has made it so enduring.

When I serve curry to friends, I'm serving four thousand years of culinary history. I'm serving trade routes and colonial legacies and immigrant creativity. I'm serving the human desire to make food more interesting, more flavorful, more alive. All of that, in a bowl of spiced sauce over rice.

sources.label: Lizzie Collingham, Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors (Oxford, 2006)

title: The Science of Fermentation: Why Humans Have Fermented Food for 10,000 Years
excerpt: From kimchi to kombucha, discover the ancient science behind fermentation and why these foods are experiencing a remarkable revival.

content.text: In the corner of my kitchen, a jar of sauerkraut is slowly bubbling. On the counter, a sourdough starter is rising and falling with the rhythm of its yeast. In the pantry, bottles of homemade hot sauce are aging, getting tangier by the day. My kitchen, like kitchens throughout human history, is alive with fermentation.

Fermentation is the oldest food technology we have. Long before we understood what bacteria were, long before we knew anything about chemistry or biology, humans figured out that certain foods, left in certain conditions, transformed into something better. Something that lasted longer, tasted more complex, and seemed to make people healthier. They didn't know why it worked. They just knew it did.
What Actually Happens

Let me explain fermentation in the simplest terms I can. Microorganisms - bacteria, yeasts, molds - eat sugars and starches in food and produce other compounds as waste products. Yeast eats sugar and produces alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is why bread rises and wine gets you tipsy. Lactic acid bacteria eat sugars and produce lactic acid, which is why yogurt is tangy and pickles are sour.

This might sound gross - we're eating bacterial waste products? - but the results are delicious. Cheese, bread, wine, beer, soy sauce, miso, kimchi, sauerkraut, chocolate, coffee, vanilla - all of these require fermentation. Take fermentation out of the human diet and you've removed most of what makes eating interesting.

content.label: Estimated age of human fermentation practices

content.text: The beauty of fermentation is that it's self-preserving. Those same acids and alcohols that create interesting flavors also prevent harmful bacteria from growing. A jar of properly fermented sauerkraut will last for months without refrigeration. Our ancestors needed this. Before we had freezers and canning, fermentation was how you made food last through winter.
Every Culture Did This

Here's what amazes me: every human culture independently discovered fermentation. In Korea, they made kimchi. In Germany, sauerkraut. In Japan, miso and soy sauce. In Ethiopia, injera bread. In Russia, kefir. In Mexico, tepache. Humans around the world, without communicating with each other, all figured out that letting food sit around and bubble made it better.
Fermentation is the oldest partnership in cooking. We set the conditions, microbes do the work, and we have been splitting the results for millennia.

I find this deeply moving. Fermentation connects us to our ancestors in a way that most cooking doesn't. When I make sauerkraut using the same basic technique people used a thousand years ago, I'm participating in something ancient and universal. Salt, cabbage, time. The recipe hasn't changed because it didn't need to.
The Gut Health Revolution

In recent years, science has caught up with tradition. Researchers studying the gut microbiome have discovered that fermented foods contain beneficial bacteria that can colonize our digestive systems and improve our health. The probiotics in yogurt, kefir, kimchi, and other fermented foods aren't just marketing buzzwords - they're living organisms that matter.

A Stanford trial gave 36 healthy adults ten weeks of either fermented foods or extra fibre. In the fermented food group, gut microbial diversity rose and nineteen inflammatory proteins in the blood fell, interleukin 6 among them. The diversity gain held for a month after the trial ended, which suggests the gut was genuinely remodelled rather than simply reflecting what had been eaten that day.

But I want to add a note of caution here. Not all fermented foods contain live bacteria. Pasteurization kills microorganisms, so most store-bought pickles and sauerkraut are not probiotic. Sourdough bread, wonderful as it is, has no live bacteria after baking. For the gut health benefits, you need raw, unpasteurized fermented foods - or you need to make them yourself.
Getting Started at Home

The good news is that fermentation is surprisingly easy. You don't need special equipment or advanced skills. The bacteria do most of the work. All you need to do is create the right conditions and then wait.

Sauerkraut is the perfect beginner project. You need cabbage, salt, a jar, and patience. Shred the cabbage, mix it with salt, pack it into a jar, and press it down so the liquid covers the cabbage. Then you wait. In a week or two, you'll have sauerkraut. It really is that simple.

Once you start fermenting, you'll find it hard to stop. The process is addictive. You start to notice opportunities everywhere - those extra vegetables could become pickles, that fruit could become vinegar, those beans could become miso. Your kitchen becomes a laboratory of transformation.

For ten thousand years, humans have been harnessing the power of microorganisms to make food better. We're still doing it today, with a bit more understanding of why it works. Every jar of kimchi, every loaf of sourdough, every glass of wine connects us to that ancient tradition. The bacteria are doing what they've always done. We're just along for the delicious ride.

title: The Fiery History of Chili Peppers: How One Plant Ignited World Cuisine
excerpt: From ancient Mexican rituals to Sichuan hotpots, trace how chili peppers spread across the globe and became essential to cultures that had never known them.

content.text: I'll never forget the first time I bit into a habanero pepper without knowing what it was. I was seventeen, working in a restaurant kitchen, and an older cook handed me this beautiful orange pepper with an innocent smile. 'Try this,' he said. I took a big bite. For the next thirty minutes, I understood physical pain in a new way. My eyes watered. My nose ran. I seriously considered calling an ambulance.

That habanero taught me something important: the chili pepper is not to be underestimated. This small fruit, capable of producing sensations ranging from pleasant warmth to screaming agony, has transformed cuisines around the world. And the craziest part? Most of the cultures we associate with spicy food - Thai, Indian, Sichuan, Korean - had never even seen a chili pepper until about five hundred years ago.
The Ancient Americas

Chili peppers are native to Mexico and Central America, where they've been cultivated for at least six thousand years. The Aztecs were serious chili enthusiasts. They used chilies in almost everything - food, medicine, religious rituals. They had words for dozens of different varieties, just as we have words for different types of wine.

When Columbus arrived in the Caribbean in 1492, he was looking for black pepper, the expensive spice from India. He found chili peppers instead and called them 'peppers' because they were hot, even though they're not related to black pepper at all. The name stuck, and we've been confused ever since.

content.label: History of chili cultivation in the Americas

content.text: I love cooking with Mexican chilies because the variety is incredible. Smoky chipotles, fruity habaneros, earthy anchos, bright serranos - each one brings something different to a dish. When I make a complex mole sauce, I might use six or seven different chilies. This was the chili culture the Spanish encountered when they arrived.
The Portuguese Spread the Fire

The Spanish brought chilies back to Europe, but it was the Portuguese who really spread them around the world. Portuguese traders carried chili seeds to Africa, India, and Southeast Asia in the early 1500s. Within a century - an incredibly short time in culinary history - chilies had become essential ingredients in cuisines across three continents.

This is remarkable when you think about it. Indian food without chilies? Thai food without heat? Sichuan food without that numbing, burning sensation? All of these cuisines existed before chilies arrived, but they've become so thoroughly integrated with chili heat that we can't imagine them any other way.
Few foods have been adopted as fast or as completely. Chillies went from unknown to indispensable across most of the world in a few generations.

Why did this happen so fast? Part of it was practical - chili plants grow easily in tropical climates and produce abundantly. Part of it was economic - chilies were cheaper than the traditional spices, making them accessible to ordinary people. But mostly, I think, people just loved the sensation. Once you develop a taste for heat, it's hard to go back.
The Science of the Burn

Here's a strange fact: the burning sensation from chilies isn't really heat. Capsaicin, the compound that makes chilies hot, doesn't actually raise the temperature in your mouth. It binds to the same receptors that detect actual heat, tricking your brain into perceiving burning when nothing is burning at all.

Even stranger: this 'pain' triggers the release of endorphins, the body's natural feel-good chemicals. That's why eating spicy food can create a kind of euphoria. It's a controlled pain, a manageable discomfort that leads to pleasure. Some researchers think this is why we enjoy spicy food despite the pain - or maybe because of it.

content.label: Scoville heat units for Pepper X, the Guinness record holder since 2023

content.text: The chase for ever-hotter peppers has become a kind of extreme sport. The Carolina Reaper held the record for years at over two million Scoville units, but it's been surpassed by even hotter varieties. These super-hot peppers are too hot to eat directly, but they've found uses in hot sauces and as novelty challenges. I don't recommend trying them without serious preparation.
Cooking with Heat

In my kitchen, I keep a variety of chilies on hand at all times. Dried chipotles for Mexican-inspired dishes. Fresh Thai bird's eye chilies for Southeast Asian cooking. Gochugaru flakes for Korean food. Calabrian chili paste for Italian. Each brings not just heat but its own distinctive flavor.

The trick to cooking with chilies is balance. Heat should enhance other flavors, not overwhelm them. A good curry has enough chili to create warmth and depth, but you should still taste the other spices, the aromatics, the base ingredients. Too much heat and everything else disappears.

I always tell new cooks to start with less chili than they think they need. You can always add more heat, but you can't take it away. And remember that different chilies affect different parts of your mouth - some hit the front of the tongue, some the back, some burn immediately while others sneak up on you.

Six thousand years after ancient Mexicans first cultivated chili peppers, we're still discovering new ways to use them. The habanero that destroyed me at seventeen is now one of my favorite ingredients - in moderation. That's the thing about chilies. They start as pain, but they end up as pleasure. You just have to respect them along the way.
